title: Settings in a client portal
metaTitle: Portal settings are a small cabinet
excerpt: Portal settings are a cabinet. Group the few things a client changes while looking for a file, such as who is notified, and bury the studio's own controls.
alt: Three hands holding coffee cups together over a wooden table, two with latte art, a small group deciding who is in the room.
caption: The useful setting is who is at the table, not a second product to learn. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs at the top of portal settings for a client?
faqs.answer: Who gets notified when a file changes, who on their team can open the project, and the name they comment under. Those are the changes a client makes while trying to keep a promised file in the right hands. Billing, API keys, and the studio's workspace tools should not appear on their screen at all.

faqs.question: Should notification settings be the only place to watch a file?
faqs.answer: The default belongs in settings, and the choice for one file can sit on that file, such as tell me when this pack changes. A client looking for a file should not have to tour a cabinet to catch the update you are about to send. Settings remember the default, and the file handles the exception.

faqs.question: How do studio settings stay out of the client cabinet?
faqs.answer: Use separate sessions: the client sees notifications, people, and their account, and the studio sees sharing defaults, templates, and integrations. Do not hide studio rows at the bottom of a client page, because someone will scroll. A client who meets a webhook form will think the portal is not for them.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Client portal settings UX is a cabinet, not a second product. A client looking for the file they were promised changes very little: who is told when a file updates, who else on their team can open it, and the name on their comments. Group those. Bury the rest. The file is the product. The cabinet is how they share it without calling you.

If the only way to hear about a new version is a long settings page, they will miss the version and search again. Put the frequent watch control on the file. Keep the default in the cabinet. Do not make them live in the cabinet to stay informed.

## What a client changes often

Notifications come first. Email me when a file is added or replaced in this project. Email the other people on the project too, or do not. A single sentence and a switch beat a matrix of event types they do not have vocabulary for. If you need more detail, open it under that sentence. Do not lead with detail.

People come next. Who on their side can view, and who can invite others. The list should use names and emails they recognize. The action is Add a teammate, with a line that says the teammate will see this project only. Removing a person should say they lose access on their next visit. Say it before they confirm. Quiet removal is how a former colleague still has the logo pack.

The name they comment under is third, and it is small. Default it to the name you already have. Let them fix a nickname without a profile essay. A required biography, a photo crop, and a role taxonomy are a social product wearing a portal's coat. Skip them unless comments are genuinely confusing without a name.

Password and email live in Account, available and not featured. Clients need them when they cannot get in. They do not need them above notifications. Sign-in help on the sign-in screen matters more than a settings row nobody opens while locked out.

Nielsen Norman Group's research, via Jakob Nielsen, says people often leave a page in 10 to 20 seconds and read only a fraction of it. A settings page that opens on a mosaic of integrations fails a client who came to add one colleague. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a practical argument for a short index: Notifications, People, Account.

## What to bury, and what to keep off their login

The studio's workspace does not belong in the client cabinet at all. Sharing defaults, file templates, webhooks, and which domains may sign in are studio operations. Put them on the studio session. A client who sees "signing secret" will either panic or paste it somewhere. Both are bad.

Billing, if the portal is not where they pay, stays out. If a particular portal really does hold invoices, put receipts on the project or under Account as a list of documents, not as a settings group full of tax forms they must complete before they can download a logo. A file and an invoice are both documents. Neither is a configuration.

Theme is optional. Honor the operating system's light or dark setting and its text size. Offer a portal theme only if brand contrast requires it. Do not make theme the first decision in a cabinet they opened to add a teammate.

Delete account, or leave project, belongs at the end of Account. Say what happens to their comments and whether the studio keeps the files. The files are the studio's delivery and the client's property in the ways your agreement already states. The button's job is to say the practical effect, not to restate a contract. "You will lose access. The studio will still have the files." is the sentence to write if that is the truth. Write the truth you actually implement.

Export can be a single action on the project, "Download everything current," rather than a settings maze. Clients think in projects. A global export of every project they ever saw is rarer. If you offer it, put it in Account and say it includes only files they can already open. Exports must not bypass permissions. An export is a search that saves to disk. Treat it with the same suspicion.

## The file still carries the urgent choice

"Tell me when this file changes" belongs on the file they were promised. That is the decision in the moment. Settings hold the default for new files. If the file switch and the default disagree, the file switch wins, and both screens use the same words. "Email me when this changes" in both places. Not "watch" on the file and "subscribe" in settings. Two words make them think one of the switches did not work.

Do not force a settings visit before the first download. Defaults should be sane. The person you invited gets email when files change. Nobody else does until they are added. Comments show the invited name. They can change any of that after they have the file. A wizard that demands a photo and a notification tour is the portal introducing itself again. The first screen already refused that idea.

When they add a teammate, send them back to the project they were in, not to a blank settings home. The landmark is the file. The cabinet is the errand. Errands return to the landmark. Show a small confirmation that names the person added. "Sam can now view Northwind." If the add failed, say so on that screen and keep the email they typed.

## Shape it for someone who did not ask for a product

Three groups. Notifications. People. Account. On a phone, that is the index. Each group is a short page. A single scrolling page of every future idea will hide "Add a teammate" under studio leftovers. You will then get the question by email, which is the workflow the portal was meant to shorten.

Switches save immediately and say Saved in text. Adding a person needs an explicit confirm because it shares the work. Those are different weights. Do not make them hunt for a global Save, and do not auto-invite on every keystroke in an email field.

Write for a client who is not in your tools all day. "Email me when a new file is added" is a full thought. "Toggle ingest notifications" is a studio thought. If a string only makes sense to the person who built the portal, it is on the wrong side of the login.

Reduced motion and larger text should work here as they do on the file list. A client who enlarges type should still see the whole notification sentence. Clipped switches get set to the wrong value. That is a real support problem dressed up as a layout nit.

## Studio settings are a different door

The studio decides default visibility, which file types are previewed, and who on the studio side is allowed to share. That cabinet can be more detailed. It still benefits from sentences and from a client preview. A toggle named "external read" is worse than "Clients can view new files without downloading."

Do not reuse the client navigation for the studio and hide items. Hidden-in-the-same-shell leaks. A separate studio home, with its own settings, keeps a client link from ever rendering a studio row. Review the client session in a browser that has never signed into the studio. Cached navigation is a classic way to see someone else's cabinet for a moment.

Keep destructive studio actions, such as revoking a whole company, at the end, named by the effect. "Remove Northwind's access" is clear. "Offboard" is not. The client cabinet does not contain that control. A client can leave. They cannot offboard their own vendor. If they need you to remove a file, that is a message, not a settings switch they should discover at midnight.

## Review the cabinet, then the next operational question

As a client, open settings from a file. Notifications and people should be the whole first screen. Add a teammate. Confirm they can open the file and cannot open another client. Turn off email. Replace the file from the studio side. Confirm the muted client does not get the email and the teammate still can, if that is what you set.

As the studio, confirm none of your integration settings render in that client session. If they do, split the cabinets before you add another field.

Once the files are findable and the right people hear about them, the next operational question is what happens when a new lead arrives, and whether the automation still sounds like a person. That piece is [automating new lead intake without losing the relationship](/blog/automating-new-lead-intake-without-losing-the-relationship). The portal cabinet should stay small. Intake is a different door.

If the client cabinet and the file screen should be designed together, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). A portal that hides the teammate list under studio settings will be used as a download link and nothing else. The relationship you wanted the portal to carry will stay in email.
